meta.title: Bebras knowledge map: 2015 example sets and 2022-23 practice challenge (Benjamin, Cadet, Junior, Senior)
meta.method: Every task in both sets was opened and solved; every answer was submitted to the site's practice checker and confirmed correct. Task descriptions, solutions and analysis are written fresh for this map; the original task wording and artwork are not reproduced. Each task links to its live page via question_url.
meta.tier_meaning: Each set lists tasks in three tiers, A, B and C, five per tier. Tiers track difficulty within an age group: A easiest, C hardest. A task reused by an older group usually drops one tier.
meta.answer_note: Multiple-choice options are shuffled between the Benjamin and Cadet copies of shared tasks, so answers are recorded by content, never by option position.
meta.prerequisite_note: Edges are marked firm (logical dependency; back up along it when a kid stalls) or tentative (usual teaching order; try other help first). Reviewed 2026-11-01 from the 23 example tasks only.

patches.method: Every task in the Junior (14-16) and Senior (16-18) 2015 example sets was opened, solved and submitted to the site's practice checker; all answers were confirmed correct. Answers that depend on counting or search (Hard Fireworks, Pirate Hunters, Bowl Factory, Spies, Building a Chip, Kangaroo, Beaver the Alchemist) were also re-derived by exhaustive computation. Descriptions are written fresh; original task wording and artwork are not reproduced.

Every task in the 2022-23 USA Bebras practice challenge for Benjamin, Cadet, Junior and Senior (31 distinct tasks, 60 slots) was opened, solved and submitted to the site's checker. 29 were marked correct on submission. Two (Hangar Carousel, Beaver Games) were confirmed against the site's published explanation after a first submission was not registered or was wrong; both answers are also re-derived by exhaustive search. Search-based answers (Hangar Carousel, Mysteria, Maze, Four Tiles, Seashells and Pebbles, Beaver Games, Virus, Treasure Box) were computed by brute force. Descriptions are my own; no task wording or artwork is reproduced. Kits and Castors were not analyzed.

Claude built a new generator family, parallel_spread (folder paint-pipes, shown as Paint Pipes), from the Virus generator candidate. It keeps the task's idea (two colours spread through a network at the same time; a tank reached by both, even one already coloured, turns to mud and stops) under an original theme and wording. Every problem passes check_parallel_spread.py, which rebuilds the network from the picture and simulates again with set-based code; corrupting the answer, the marked option, a starting colour or a pipe is caught in all 720 mutation trials.

Claude built a new generator family, code_clues (folder code-lock, shown as Code Lock), from the Treasure Box generator candidate. It keeps the task's idea (find the code that agrees with every guess's right-spot and wrong-spot feedback) under an original theme, symbols and wording. Levels 1-3 offer four codes; levels 4-5 ask the student to build the code, and the clues always leave exactly one. Every problem passes check_code_clues.py, which rescores the answer against each clue with its own code, enumerates every possible code to confirm only one fits, and re-derives every wrong answer's tags; corrupting the answer, a clue's feedback, the clue list or a tag is caught in all 300 mutation trials.

Claude built a new generator family, brick_rule (folder brick-pyramid, shown as Brick Pyramid), from the Colorful Tower generator candidate. It keeps the task's idea (a three-colour pyramid where a brick and the two under it are all the same or all different) under an original theme and wording, and adds two kinds of question the source task does not ask: counting one colour in the finished pyramid, and working backward to hidden bottom bricks. At level 5 the shown bricks always allow a step-by-step deduction (a brick and one brick under it force the other), and the explanation walks through it. Every problem passes check_brick_rule.py, which rebuilds the pyramid from the picture and solves it with arithmetic mod 3; every corrupted answer key is caught in the mutation trials. For colouring questions the server tags each wrong brick from the student's own bricks below it.

Claude built a new generator family, friend_reach (folder pass-it-on, shown as Pass It On), from the Popularity generator candidate. It keeps the task's idea (a person's reach is everyone within two steps, and the person with the most friends is not always the one who reaches the most) under an original story, where news is passed on exactly twice, with its own names and pictures. It adds two kinds of question the source task does not ask: counting who hears one person's news, and choosing the one new friendship that makes a person's news reach everyone. Every problem passes check_friend_reach.py, which rebuilds the graph from the picture, checks that no line runs through a person it does not join, and solves again with breadth-first search; every corrupted answer key is caught in the mutation trials. Claude also marked two older candidates as built: Hard Fireworks has been covered by signal_code (Signal Lamp) and Building a Chip by grid_routes (Robot Routes) since before candidate status was tracked.

Claude built a new generator family, stone_hops (folder frog-hops, shown as Frog Hops), from the Kangaroo generator candidate. It keeps the task's idea (a jumper with one forward and one back jump size must land on every position exactly once, and the search needs forced moves plus backing out of dead ends) under an original story, a frog on stepping stones, with our own wording and pictures. It adds water gaps, which the source does not have; they vary the puzzles and make the hop arithmetic count spots rather than stones. Claude found that with only two hops every puzzle that needs backtracking has exactly one full trip, and that the space is small (tens of puzzles per size), so the generator lists every valid puzzle for a level and seeds index into that list. It adds two kinds of question the source does not ask: picking the one list of stones that follows the rules, and tapping out the whole trip, which the server grades by playing it back. Every problem passes check_stone_hops.py, which rebuilds the row from the picture and counts full trips again with bitmask dynamic programming; every corrupted answer key is caught in the mutation trials.

Claude wrote one short question for the student per misconception tag that the generators or the answer checker can produce (87 tags). The practice page shows it after a wrong try with that tag. Each question points at the likely mistake without giving the answer away.

domains.name: Algorithms and programming
domains.covers: executing, writing and reasoning about step-by-step procedures, loops, conditionals, search and optimization

domains.name: Data, structures and representation
domains.covers: how information is encoded and organized: binary, sequences, trees, graphs, schemas

domains.name: Logic and constraints
domains.covers: boolean conditions, constraint satisfaction, elimination, ordering from partial information

domains.name: Processes and systems
domains.covers: state over time, simulation, scheduling, pipelines, periodic behavior

domains.name: Computers and society
domains.covers: security awareness, privacy, licensing and intellectual property, judging online information; tasks with no algorithm where the skill is reading a situation or a rule set precisely

concepts.name: Executing a sequence of instructions
concepts.description: Apply instructions one at a time, updating state after each, without skipping or merging steps.
concepts.observable_signs: Student can trace a short program and report the state after each step.
tutor_moves: Have the student write the state after every step in a table.
Ask what changes and what stays the same at each step.

concepts.name: State and state change

prerequisites.reason: State can be grasped from a static picture; tracing instructions is the usual way in, not a requirement.

concepts.description: A system is described by a small set of variables; each operation maps one state to the next.
concepts.observable_signs: Student names the variables that matter (positions, contents, who is ahead) and ignores decoration.
tutor_moves: Ask: what would you need to write down to pause and resume this exactly?

concepts.name: Simulation

prerequisites.reason: Simulation is updating state event by event.

concepts.description: Step through events in order and track how state evolves, rather than guessing the end result.
concepts.observable_signs: Student processes events in the given order and keeps a running record.
tutor_moves: Insist on one event at a time.
Compare the student's guess with the simulated result to show why simulation is needed.

concepts.name: Writing a program to reach a goal

prerequisites.reason: Must read programs before writing them.
Planning needs a model of what each command changes.

concepts.description: Choose and order commands from a fixed instruction set so the final state meets a goal and any postconditions.
concepts.observable_signs: Student plans before acting and checks the postcondition, not just the main goal.
tutor_moves: Ask for the goal state in words first.
Ask which part of the goal is easy to forget (for example, returning to start).

concepts.name: Swap using temporary storage

prerequisites.reason: The swap is a planned command sequence.

concepts.description: Exchanging two items when only one can move at a time needs a third place to park one of them.
concepts.observable_signs: Student identifies the empty slot as essential before moving anything.
tutor_moves: Ask what happens if you move A straight onto B's spot.

concepts.name: Loops and repetition

prerequisites.reason: A loop body is a sequence.
Needed when the task is to write the body; reading a loop does not need it.

concepts.description: A repeated body produces a repeating output; finding the body means finding the period of the output.
concepts.observable_signs: Student finds the smallest repeating unit and its correct starting phase.
tutor_moves: Ask the student to mark where the pattern starts repeating.
Ask how many steps one repeat should advance.

concepts.name: Conditionals and branching

prerequisites.reason: Branching is a step in executing a program.

concepts.description: IF/ELSE chooses one path; nested conditionals reach an inner branch only when outer conditions fail.
concepts.observable_signs: Student can state the full condition for reaching any branch, including negated outer tests.
tutor_moves: Ask: to get here, which earlier tests had to be false?
Probe equality cases explicitly.

concepts.name: Nested conditionals

prerequisites.reason: Nesting builds on single IF/ELSE.
Reaching an inner branch means an outer test was false; that negation is where errors happen.

concepts.description: An IF inside an ELSE (or THEN) is reached only when the outer test came out a particular way; the full condition for a branch includes every test above it.
concepts.observable_signs: Student states the complete path condition for a branch, including the outer tests that had to fail.
tutor_moves: Ask: to reach this line, which tests above it had to be true or false?
Have the student write the path condition before checking any option.

concepts.name: Boolean AND filtering
concepts.description: An item qualifies only if every condition holds; one failed condition rejects it.
concepts.observable_signs: Student checks all conditions on each candidate instead of stopping at the first match.
tutor_moves: Make a checklist grid: candidates as rows, conditions as columns.

concepts.name: Negation and boundary cases

prerequisites.reason: Earlier version put this under CONDITIONALS; Dream Dress shows the boundary skill appears without any program. Linked to AND because thresholds first show up as filter conditions.

concepts.description: The opposite of 'greater than' is 'less than or equal'; 'more than 3' excludes 3. Ties and edges decide many answers.
concepts.observable_signs: Student handles equal values and exact thresholds correctly.
tutor_moves: Ask what happens when the two values are equal.
Ask whether exactly 3 counts.

concepts.name: Constraint satisfaction

prerequisites.reason: Satisfying several constraints at once is AND over a configuration.

concepts.description: Find a configuration that meets several conditions at once, often by fixing the most constrained part first.
concepts.observable_signs: Student starts from the tightest constraint and propagates its consequences.
tutor_moves: Ask which requirement leaves the fewest choices.
Ask what a decision here forces elsewhere.
notes: 2022-23 adds forced propagation tasks (Colorful Tower, Beehive, Flower Garden/minesweeper, Treasure Box/mastermind).

concepts.name: Elimination and case analysis

prerequisites.reason: Elimination rejects options failing any condition; kids eliminate informally before they can state AND.

concepts.description: Rule out options that violate any condition; when a mapping is unstated, test each possible assignment.
concepts.observable_signs: Student tries both readings of an ambiguous assignment and discards the contradictory one.
tutor_moves: Ask whether the picture actually says which item belongs to whom.

concepts.name: Ordering from partial information
concepts.description: Pairwise facts (A before B, A above B) combine into a total order; the answer must satisfy every pair.
concepts.observable_signs: Student lists each pairwise relation before choosing an order.
tutor_moves: Have the student write every overlap as 'X before Y' and then check each option against the list.

concepts.name: Topological ordering

prerequisites.reason: Topological order is ordering from pairwise relations.

concepts.description: Order items so every dependency comes first; layering, stacking and recipe steps are all instances.
concepts.observable_signs: Student builds the order from items with no unmet dependencies.
tutor_moves: Ask which item could only have been placed first.
Ask which item could only have been placed last.

concepts.name: Sorted lists and partitions

prerequisites.reason: Needs a sorted list to partition.

concepts.description: In a sorted list, a rule like 'every A is at or below every B' means the A group is a prefix; ties locate the cut.
concepts.observable_signs: Student realizes the groups split the sorted list at one point.
tutor_moves: Ask where in the sorted list the boundary could be.

concepts.name: Linear vs cyclic sequences
concepts.description: A ring has no start and can be read in either direction, so two rings match if one is a rotation or reflection of the other.
concepts.observable_signs: Student anchors on one element and reads neighbors in both directions.
tutor_moves: Ask the student to pick one bead and name its two neighbors in each option.

concepts.name: Binary place value
concepts.description: Each position is worth double the previous; the highest set bit outweighs all lower bits combined.
concepts.observable_signs: Student compares from the most significant position down instead of summing everything.
tutor_moves: Ask which single square is worth the most.
Ask whether all the other squares together can beat it.

concepts.name: Bits and combinations of states

prerequisites.reason: Reading on/off combinations from a truth table does not need place value; counting the 2^n states does.

concepts.description: n on/off switches give 2^n states; a truth table maps each combination to an outcome.
concepts.observable_signs: Student reads each switch independently and combines them per time step.
tutor_moves: Ask how many different combinations three lights can make, and why.

concepts.name: Periodic behavior

prerequisites.reason: Timelines are state over time, but kids handle repeating patterns early.

concepts.description: Repeating on/off cycles with different periods can be laid out as parallel timelines; together they act like counter bits.
concepts.observable_signs: Student draws one timeline per signal before combining.
tutor_moves: Ask for a row per light and a column per minute.

concepts.name: Encoding and decoding

prerequisites.reason: Encoding is applying steps in order.

concepts.description: A message passes through a pipeline of reversible transformations; decoding applies the inverses in reverse order.
concepts.observable_signs: Student undoes the last step first.
tutor_moves: Ask what the last thing done to the word was.
Offer the shortcut: encode each answer option forward and compare.
notes: 2022-23 Cipher 8: rotation relative to the current pointer (delta encoding), so repeated letters cost 0.

concepts.name: Composition and inverse functions

prerequisites.reason: Pedagogical order (concrete ciphers before the general idea), not a logical dependency.

concepts.description: Doing f then g is undone by g-inverse then f-inverse; order matters.
concepts.observable_signs: Student can explain why order reverses on the way back.
tutor_moves: Use the socks-and-shoes analogy.

concepts.name: Postfix notation and stacks

prerequisites.reason: Evaluation is left-to-right execution.
The stack is the state.

concepts.description: In postfix, operands come first and the operator follows; a stack evaluates it left to right with no parentheses needed.
concepts.observable_signs: Student converts an infix expression by building sub-results innermost-first.
tutor_moves: Ask which operation in the expression must happen first.
Have the student simulate the stack with written boxes.

concepts.name: Trees and hierarchies
concepts.description: A root branches into children; leaves have no children; there is exactly one path between any two nodes.
concepts.observable_signs: Student traces from root to leaf and reasons about subtrees.
tutor_moves: Ask what is downstream of this point.

concepts.name: Schemas and multiplicity constraints

prerequisites.reason: A schema is a tree with counts on edges.

concepts.description: A hierarchy diagram with allowed counts per child defines which structures are valid, like a grammar or data schema.
concepts.observable_signs: Student checks lower bounds (required items) as well as upper bounds.
tutor_moves: Ask which thing in the diagram is required, not optional.

concepts.name: Binary search trees

prerequisites.reason: A BST is a tree.
Search relies on comparison order.

concepts.description: Every left subtree holds smaller keys and every right subtree larger ones, so each comparison discards half the remaining tree.
concepts.observable_signs: Student infers the left-smaller/right-larger rule from a few moves and then searches directly.
tutor_moves: Ask the student to compare the numbers in the left and right rooms with the current room.

concepts.name: Modeling a picture as a graph
concepts.description: Places become nodes, connections become edges, costs become weights; the decoration drops away.
concepts.observable_signs: Student redraws the scene as dots and lines.
tutor_moves: Ask the student to sketch the scene with only dots and lines.

concepts.name: Graph isomorphism and invariants

prerequisites.reason: Must see the figure as nodes and edges to compare structure.

concepts.description: Bending a figure changes its shape but not who is connected to whom; node count and degree sequence must match.
concepts.observable_signs: Student counts nodes and connections per node instead of comparing silhouettes.
tutor_moves: Ask how many sticks touch each nut.
notes: Junior Word Chains requires producing the label mapping, not just detecting a match.

concepts.name: Path tracing

prerequisites.reason: Kids trace maps without abstracting them; the abstraction helps with harder maps.

concepts.description: Follow a route through a network against a description of turns and stop counts.
concepts.observable_signs: Student checks each candidate route against every clue in order.
tutor_moves: Have the student trace each line with a finger while counting stops.

concepts.name: Reachability through switches

prerequisites.reason: Gate networks are trees.
Needed only when gate choices interact.

concepts.description: With gates on edges, a node receives flow if some open path reaches it; closing a gate cuts off everything below it.
concepts.observable_signs: Student reasons about whole subtrees when deciding a gate.
tutor_moves: Ask: if this gate is open, which fields get water?
notes: Junior Irrigation System extends this to a DAG with two-way switches (each gate always sends water one way or the other) and ungated forks that feed both sides.

concepts.name: Shortest (cheapest) path

prerequisites.reason: Needs the weighted-graph view.
Following candidate routes precedes comparing their costs.

concepts.description: Minimize total weight from source to target; the cheapest first step is often not on the best path.
concepts.observable_signs: Student records the best known cost to each node and improves it, rather than committing greedily.
tutor_moves: Ask for the cheapest cost to reach each island from the bank.
Show a greedy path that ends up worse.
notes: Senior Building a Chip asks for the number of shortest paths on a grid with obstacles (see COUNTING_DP).
2022-23 Maze: two maze floors with a costly switch between them; state is (floor, cell) and a route with two switches beats staying on one floor.

concepts.name: State-space search and minimality

prerequisites.reason: Search is over states.
Simulating one sequence precedes comparing many.

concepts.description: Enumerate states reachable in 1, 2, 3 moves; the first level that contains the goal gives the minimum, and earlier levels prove nothing shorter works.
concepts.observable_signs: Student shows that no shorter sequence works, not just that one sequence works.
tutor_moves: Ask: could it be done in fewer moves? How do you know?

concepts.name: Invariants

prerequisites.reason: Spotting what stays constant needs a sense of what changes.

concepts.description: Some quantity never changes (total liquid, edge count, ordering rule); using it prunes impossible options.
concepts.observable_signs: Student names what stays constant and uses it to reject options.
tutor_moves: Ask what stays the same no matter what you do.
notes: 2022-23 Tic-Tac-Toe: a final board is valid only if counts differ by at most one, the game is over, and the winner moved last.

concepts.name: Dependencies, critical path and parallelism

prerequisites.reason: Scheduling respects dependency order.

concepts.description: Tasks with prerequisites form a DAG; with unlimited workers the finish time is the longest dependency chain, so extra workers stop helping.
concepts.observable_signs: Student finds the longest chain and sees that it bounds every schedule.
tutor_moves: Ask which chain of steps can never overlap.
Ask what a fourth burner would do.

concepts.name: Minimal change between states

prerequisites.reason: Comparing states attribute by attribute.

concepts.description: Neighbor states differ in exactly one attribute; ordering them is finding a path where each step flips one feature.
concepts.observable_signs: Student lists the attributes and compares items attribute by attribute.
tutor_moves: Have the student list each picture's features in a row and compare adjacent rows.

concepts.name: Directions and coordinates
concepts.description: Compass directions are relative positions; 'X is due east of me' fixes the row, 'NE' requires both up and right.
concepts.observable_signs: Student converts each clue into a constraint on position.
tutor_moves: Ask where you would have to stand for that arrow to be correct.
notes: 2022-23 Listen and Walk: left/front/right relative to the walker's own heading, which turns; position and heading are both state.

concepts.name: Recognizing online fraud
concepts.description: Spot the pattern of a scam: an offer that is too good, pressure to pay before anything can be checked, and 'proof' that proves nothing (a scanned ID can be forged or stolen).
concepts.observable_signs: Student names which part of the message cannot be verified and why it matters.
tutor_moves: Ask: what could the sender fake, and what would you need to see before paying?
Ask what a copy of an ID actually proves about the person sending it.

concepts.name: Licenses and permitted use
concepts.description: A license grants some actions and forbids others; the forbidden action is often distributing a changed version, not making one or charging for copies.
concepts.observable_signs: Student separates what is done (copy, change, sell) from who receives it (kept private vs shared).
tutor_moves: Make a two-column table: actions the license allows, actions it forbids. Check each option against it.
Ask whether making something and sharing it are the same action under the rule.

concepts.name: Recursion and recursive definitions

prerequisites.reason: Recursive structures in these tasks are trees or DAGs.
Unfolding a definition step by step uses the same habit as tracing.

concepts.description: Something is defined in terms of smaller versions of itself: a person's abilities in terms of a parent's, an item's cost in terms of its ingredients, a mobile in terms of sub-mobiles.
concepts.observable_signs: Student solves the smallest pieces first and reuses those results to build larger ones.
tutor_moves: Ask: what do you need to know first before you can answer for this one?
Have the student write the answer for each leaf, then for each level up.

concepts.name: Totals over a dependency graph

prerequisites.reason: Each item's total is defined from its inputs' totals.
Working bottom-up is a topological order.

concepts.description: Compute a total (cost, count) for each item from the totals of the items it is made from, once each, from the bottom up. Like a bill of materials.
concepts.observable_signs: Student computes and records each intermediate total once and reuses it.
tutor_moves: Ask the student to write each intermediate item's base cost next to it before tackling the final item.

concepts.name: Parsing nested notation

prerequisites.reason: Brackets inside brackets describe parts inside parts.
The parse is a tree.

concepts.description: Turn a bracketed expression into the structure it describes by matching brackets and reading each bracket as one node with its children.
concepts.observable_signs: Student matches brackets correctly and can draw the tree from the text.
tutor_moves: Have the student underline each matching bracket pair in a different color.
Ask for the top level first: how many things hang from the top stick?

concepts.name: Modular arithmetic and cycles

prerequisites.reason: Counting around a circle is the concrete form of working mod n.

concepts.description: Stepping k places around n positions visits i, i+k, i+2k, ... wrapping around; whether every position is visited depends on gcd(n, k).
concepts.observable_signs: Student counts a step size on a circular drawing correctly and can predict one loop vs several.
tutor_moves: Number the dots, then follow one line and count how many numbers it skips.

concepts.name: Neighborhoods and distance in graphs

prerequisites.reason: Distance is measured along edges.

concepts.description: The set of nodes within k steps of a node; for many real rules (who can see a post) the relevant reach is 2 steps, not 1.
concepts.observable_signs: Student derives the right distance from the rule before counting.
tutor_moves: Ask: who can see this person's page? And who can see the pages this person posted on?

concepts.name: Ambiguous and prefix-free codes

prerequisites.reason: Codes as mappings from symbols to words.

concepts.description: When one codeword can be the start of another and there are no separators, a received signal can split into words in several ways. Prefix-free codes avoid this.
concepts.observable_signs: Student finds more than one valid split and can say which property of the code causes it.
tutor_moves: Ask whether any codeword starts with another codeword.
Ask for a second way to split the signal after the student finds one.

concepts.name: Counting by building up partial counts

prerequisites.reason: Partial counts are attached to positions or states.

concepts.description: Count the ways to reach the end by recording, for each position, how many ways reach it, and adding those for the next position. Avoids listing every possibility.
concepts.observable_signs: Student writes a number at each position or node rather than enumerating paths by hand.
tutor_moves: Ask: how many ways are there to reach just this point? Write it down, then move one step on.
Point out the shortcut on a small grid by comparing with a full listing.

concepts.name: Game trees and optimal play

prerequisites.reason: Positions are states and moves are transitions.
For-all and there-exists reasoning over replies.

concepts.description: Under optimal play, a side wins only if it has a move that works against every reply. Winning against a careless opponent proves nothing.
concepts.observable_signs: Student asks what the opponent's best reply is, not just whether a win is possible.
tutor_moves: Play the opponent's side yourself and always pick the best escape.
Ask: does your plan still work if the other side never makes a mistake?
notes: 2022-23 Seashells and Pebbles: a misère placement game on a graph; the unique winning move is an isolated leaf that wastes a turn and passes the shortage of safe holes to the opponent.

concepts.name: Proving something cannot be done

prerequisites.reason: Most impossibility arguments rest on something that never changes or a bound that cannot be beaten.

concepts.description: Show that no sequence of moves reaches a goal, or that no faster schedule exists, by an argument (an invariant, a counting bound, a parity reason) rather than by failing to find one.
concepts.observable_signs: Student gives a reason that covers every possible attempt, not a list of attempts that failed.
tutor_moves: Ask: how much can change in one move or one round at most?
Ask what stays the same after every move.

concepts.name: Spreading information in parallel rounds

prerequisites.reason: Each person's knowledge is state.
Rounds are simulated in order.

concepts.description: When people meet in pairs each round, what anyone knows can at most double per round, which sets a minimum number of rounds; an odd group wastes a seat every round.
concepts.observable_signs: Student gives both a schedule and a reason it cannot be shorter.
tutor_moves: Ask: after one round, what is the most anyone can know? After two?
Ask what happens to the person without a partner.
notes: 2022-23 Virus: two infections spread at once; a node reached by both on the same day is destroyed and blocks further spread (multi-source BFS with ties as walls). The two sources are neighbours, so they destroy each other on day 1.

concepts.name: Passes of adjacent swaps

prerequisites.reason: Each pass is simulated swap by swap.
Swaps fix out-of-order neighbors.

concepts.description: One pass of neighbor swaps carries one extreme element all the way but moves others by at most one place, so the number of passes depends on how far the slowest element must travel.
concepts.observable_signs: Student distinguishes passes from swaps and simulates the pass in the stated direction.
tutor_moves: Ask: in one pass, how far can the smallest bowl move? How far can the largest?

concepts.name: Backtracking search

prerequisites.reason: Backtracking explores a state space depth-first.

concepts.description: Try a choice, continue until stuck, undo the last choice and try the next. Forced moves and early dead ends shrink the search quickly.
concepts.observable_signs: Student keeps track of where they backed up and notices forced moves.
tutor_moves: Ask: from here, how many moves are possible? If only one, take it without guessing.
notes: 2022-23 Listen and Walk and Four Tiles need trying a branch and backing out when a later clue fails.

concepts.name: Parity check bits

prerequisites.reason: Locating the error is elimination over rows and columns.

concepts.description: Extra marks are added so every row and column holds an even count; a change shows up as an odd row and an odd column, and their crossing locates it. The idea behind error-detecting and error-correcting codes.
concepts.observable_signs: Student counts each row and column and reasons from which ones are odd, rather than guessing cells.
tutor_moves: Ask which rows are odd now, and which columns.
Ask: if one mark disappeared, how many rows would change from even to odd?

concepts.name: Grammars and rewriting rules

prerequisites.reason: Rules that refer to themselves build nested structure.
A derivation is a sequence of rule applications.

concepts.description: A start symbol grows by applying rewriting rules; a string belongs to the language if some sequence of rules produces it. Deciding membership is easiest backward: undo a rule whose result is visible, repeat until reaching the start or getting stuck.
concepts.observable_signs: Student works backward from the string and can show the derivation, or explains why every backward step gets stuck.
tutor_moves: Ask which rule could have made the last part of this string.
Ask: if you undo that rule, what is left?

concepts.name: Cycles in a sequence of states

prerequisites.reason: The cycle is found by stepping states forward.
Positions on a loop repeat with the loop length.

concepts.description: A process that moves through finitely many states must eventually loop; a slow and a fast runner on the same path meet inside the loop (Floyd's tortoise and hare).
concepts.observable_signs: Student separates the lead-in from the loop and reasons about the gap between runners modulo the loop length.
tutor_moves: Ask how far apart the runners are after each minute once both are on the loop.

concepts.name: Logic gates and circuits

prerequisites.reason: AND is the first gate; XOR and OR follow.

concepts.description: Signals combine through AND (both), OR (at least one) and XOR (exactly one) gates in a tree. To make the output true, work backward from it: an AND needs both inputs, an XOR needs exactly one.
concepts.observable_signs: Student distinguishes 'only one' (XOR) from 'at least one' (OR) and works from the output back to the inputs.
tutor_moves: Ask what this gate needs from its two inputs for the light to come on.
Ask what happens to an 'only one' gate if both inputs are on.

concepts.name: Matching with a counter or stack

prerequisites.reason: The bucket count is state carried along the sequence.

concepts.description: Items that open and close (nuts and bolts, brackets) are valid when a running count never drops below zero and ends at zero.
concepts.observable_signs: Student checks the running count at every step, not only the totals.
tutor_moves: Ask what is in the bucket after each item.
Ask: is having equal numbers of nuts and bolts enough?

concepts.name: Indirection and indexing

prerequisites.reason: Nested lookups are done one at a time.
A nested lookup is a composition of functions.

concepts.description: A value is used as a position for the next lookup (a[a[i]], pointers). Nested expressions are evaluated inside-out.
concepts.observable_signs: Student evaluates the innermost lookup first and keeps track of which list each step uses.
tutor_moves: Ask which part of the expression can be worked out right now.
Ask: is this number a position or a value?

concepts.name: Finding the best with comparisons

prerequisites.reason: Each comparison eliminates the losers.

concepts.description: Every comparison of k items eliminates at most k-1 of them, and the best is the only item never beaten; so q comparisons of k find the best among at most 1 + q(k-1) items. Knockout tournaments achieve the bound.
concepts.observable_signs: Student counts eliminations rather than items looked at, and carries the winner forward.
tutor_moves: Ask how many gems each question rules out.
Ask whether the winner of the first group has to be asked about again.

concepts.name: Bounds that prove an answer is best

prerequisites.reason: A bound shows nothing better can exist.

concepts.description: Before searching, compute what no solution can beat (total area, eliminations per step, presses per move); a solution that meets the bound is optimal.
concepts.observable_signs: Student states the bound first and then shows a solution that reaches it.
tutor_moves: Ask: what is the best you could possibly hope for, and why?
Ask whether your answer reaches that limit.

concepts.name: Worst-case thinking

prerequisites.reason: Worst case is the reverse question to cheapest route.

concepts.description: Find the input or order that makes a process as slow as possible; often the greedy 'go to the farthest remaining' choice builds it.
concepts.observable_signs: Student asks which choice would hurt most at each step and checks that the first choice is not fixed.
tutor_moves: Ask which plane would take the longest to bring to the gate first.

concepts.name: Nearest-neighbour regions

prerequisites.reason: Distance on a grid builds on coordinates.

concepts.description: Each cell takes the label of the closest (or farthest) marked point, which splits a grid into regions; ties are a separate case.
concepts.observable_signs: Student predicts region shapes around points without computing every cell.
tutor_moves: Ask which dot a cell in the corner is closest to.
Ask what the picture would look like if the rule were 'farthest'.

concepts.name: Dominance and Pareto optimality

prerequisites.reason: 'No one rates another higher' is a for-all condition.

concepts.description: An option is a favorite only if, for every person, nothing is rated higher. Changing one person's top rating changes which options count.
concepts.observable_signs: Student checks the condition person by person and considers lowering ratings as well as raising them.
tutor_moves: Ask what this friend's highest rating is.
Ask whether you could make this friend happy with every movie at once.

concepts.name: Edge-matching and tiling

prerequisites.reason: Each shared side is a constraint between two tiles.

concepts.description: Tiles with a symbol on each side must touch only at equal symbols; rotation is allowed. Counting how often each symbol appears prunes the search.
concepts.observable_signs: Student uses rare symbols to fix tiles to the outside and tries rotations systematically.
tutor_moves: Ask which symbols appear on only one tile.
Ask which two sides of a corner tile touch other tiles.

reasoning_moves.name: Work backward from the known end
Test each option against every condition
Start with the most constrained piece
Exhaust a small space to prove minimality
Infer a hidden rule by exploring
Check a candidate by running it forward

tasks.title: Bracelet
tasks.scenario: A broken bracelet lies as a straight string of six distinct beads. Four intact ring bracelets are shown; pick the one it came from.
tasks.what_it_tests: Recognizing that a circular arrangement is the same under rotation and reflection, while adjacency must be preserved.
solution: Pick one bead in the string and note its two neighbors (the end beads become neighbors of each other once the ring closes).
For each ring, read the order starting from that bead, clockwise and counterclockwise.
Keep the ring whose order matches the string in one of the two directions.
tasks.answer: The ring whose bead order, read counterclockwise from the square, is square, circle, pentagon, star, triangle, cross. In both sets it is the ring with the triangle at the top and the star just clockwise of it.
common_errors: Requiring the string's first bead to be at the top of the ring.
Reading only clockwise and rejecting the mirrored match.
Missing a swap of two adjacent beads in a distractor.
difficulty_drivers: Whether distractors differ by one adjacent swap
Whether a reflected match is the answer
hint_ladder: Does a ring have a first bead?
Pick the square. Which beads sit on either side of it on the string?
Check that pair of neighbors on each ring.

params.distractors: adjacent swap, non-adjacent swap, one bead moved

generator_template.validity: Exactly one option is a rotation or reflection of the string closed into a ring.

tasks.title: Trams
tasks.scenario: Several numbered tram lines leave a shared depot on a schematic map. A trip is described only by stop counts and turns; identify which line was ridden.
tasks.what_it_tests: Matching a described route to paths on a network diagram.
solution: Follow each line from the depot, counting stops.
Keep lines that turn after the stated count and turn again at the next stop.
Of those, keep the line that reaches its destination after the final stated count.
tasks.answer: Line 6.
common_errors: Counting the depot as a stop.
Treating a shared trunk as a turn.
Stopping after the first matching clue.
difficulty_drivers: Lines that match all but the last clue
hint_ladder: Which lines go straight for the first three stops?
Which of those turn twice in a row?
Count the remaining stops for each.

generator_template.validity: Exactly one line satisfies the full clue sequence; at least one line satisfies all but the last clue.

tasks.title: Beaver Dam
tasks.scenario: A central lake feeds a branching network of canals down to fields at the edges. Gates on canal segments can be opened or closed. Some fields must get water, others must stay dry; set the gates.
tasks.what_it_tests: Reachability in a tree with switches on edges, and constraint satisfaction when one gate controls several leaves.
solution: Trace each canal from the lake to every field it can reach.
A gate whose downstream area includes a dry field with no closable gate in between must stay closed.
Route water to each flower field through gates that do not also feed a dry field.
Leave all other gates closed.
tasks.answer: Open exactly 4 of the 12 gates: the top lake gate (its branch feeds the top flower field; close the side gate toward the dry field), the lower-left lake gate (feeds the left and lower-middle flower fields; keep its side gate toward the large dry field closed), the right lake gate, and the first gate on its right fork toward the upper-right flower field (keep the next gate toward the dry field closed). The upper-left lake gate must stay closed because its branch reaches a dry field with no gate in between.
common_errors: Opening every gate on a path to a flower field without checking side branches.
Assuming each field has only one supply route.
Not noticing that a flower field reachable from a forbidden gate can be fed another way.
difficulty_drivers: Branches that mix wanted and unwanted fields
hint_ladder: Pick a dry field. Which gates, if opened, would send water to it?
Is there a flower field that can only be reached one way?
Can the left flower field be fed from more than one lake gate?

generator_template.validity: At least one gate setting works; at least one tempting gate must be closed.

tasks.title: Mushrooms
tasks.scenario: Three walkers stand on a small grid with obstacles and target cells. Three short move programs made of straight and diagonal steps are given, but the grid does not say which walker runs which program. Place each walker where it ends.
tasks.what_it_tests: Executing relative-move programs on a grid and matching programs to start positions.
solution: Run each program from each start position.
Discard runs that leave the grid or land on an obstacle.
Keep the one-to-one assignment where every walker ends on a target.
tasks.answer: On a 5x5 grid (rows and columns numbered from 0 at top-left): the walker at row 0, col 1 runs SE, NE, SE and ends at row 1, col 4; the walker at row 2, col 2 runs NW, S, SW and ends at row 3, col 0; the walker at row 3, col 4 runs SW, NW, S and ends at row 4, col 2.
common_errors: Assuming the program order matches the walkers' order on the grid.
Confusing diagonal directions.
Not checking intermediate cells for obstacles or the grid edge.
hint_ladder: Can every program start from every walker?
Which program walks off the grid from the top walker?
Once one pairing is fixed, what remains?

generator_template.validity: Exactly one bijection of programs to walkers keeps every path legal and ends on targets.

tasks.title: Setting the Table
tasks.scenario: A top-down picture shows overlapping tableware on a cloth. Choose the order in which the objects were laid down.
tasks.what_it_tests: Turning visual occlusion into precedence relations and finding the order consistent with all of them.
solution: For each overlapping pair, the object on top was placed later.
List every such pair.
Pick the option consistent with all pairs.
tasks.answer: Cloth, cup and saucer, napkin, plate, knife.
common_errors: Missing a small overlap (here the napkin edge lies over the saucer).
Ordering by size or habit instead of by what is visibly on top.
tasks.analyst_note: I picked cloth, napkin, cup, plate, knife on the first try and it was wrong; the napkin-over-saucer overlap is easy to miss at normal zoom. Expect students to make the same mistake.
hint_ladder: What is at the very bottom?
What is on top of everything?
Look closely where the napkin meets the saucer.

generator_template.validity: Overlap pairs determine a unique total order; each distractor violates at least one pair.

tasks.title: Animal Competition
tasks.scenario: Nine competitors from two groups have known sorted scores with two tied pairs. Every member of one group scored at or below every member of the other; exactly one cross-group tie exists, and one other tie is within the lower group. Count the lower group.
tasks.what_it_tests: Partitioning a sorted list with a threshold rule and using ties to place the boundary.
solution: The lower group is a prefix of the sorted scores.
The cross-group tie means the boundary splits a tied pair.
The other tied pair must be entirely inside the lower group, so the boundary is at the higher tie.
Count the prefix up to and including the lower member of that tie.
common_errors: Splitting at the lower tie, which leaves the other tie straddling nothing.
Treating 'no lower-group member scored more than any upper-group member' as strict.
difficulty_drivers: Whether the rule is strict or not
hint_ladder: If every dog is at or below every beaver, where are the dogs in the sorted list?
Which tie could be split between a dog and a beaver?
Where must the dog-dog tie be?

generator_template.validity: Exactly one cut position satisfies all tie clues.

tasks.title: Geocaching
tasks.scenario: A map shows two targets and four landmarks. Two people stand together; their direction finders point due east and northeast toward their respective targets, but the screens are not labeled with owners. Which landmark are they at?
tasks.what_it_tests: Converting compass directions into position constraints and testing both possible owner assignments.
solution: For each landmark, find the direction to each target.
Look for a landmark where one target is due east and the other is northeast.
Note that assigning the screens in the order the people are named makes the clues contradictory; the other assignment works.
tasks.answer: The mushroom landmark (the second target is due east of it; the first target is northeast).
common_errors: Assuming the top screen belongs to the first-named person.
Treating northeast as 'roughly up'.
hint_ladder: Does the picture say whose screen is whose?
Where could you stand so that one target is exactly east?
Is the other target northeast from there?

generator_template.validity: Exactly one landmark satisfies both arrows under some owner assignment.

tasks.title: Crane Operating
tasks.scenario: An overhead crane over three floor slots holds two crates in the outer slots. Using six commands (left, right, up, down, catch, release), swap the crates and park the crane where it started.
tasks.what_it_tests: Writing a sequential program with a swap through a temporary location and a postcondition.
solution: Move crate A to the empty middle slot.
Move crate B to A's old slot.
Move A from the middle to B's old slot.
Return the crane to its start position.
tasks.answer: One working 24-command program: down, catch, up, right, down, release, up; right, down, catch, up, left, left, down, release, up; right, down, catch, up, right, down, release, up; left, left.
common_errors: Trying to move A straight onto B.
Forgetting to lift before moving sideways.
Forgetting to return the crane.
Confusing the catch and release icons (in this interface the open claw is release).
hint_ladder: Where can you put a crate while you move the other one?
Write the three crate moves first, then fill in crane steps.
Where must the crane end?

generator_template.validity: Goal reachable; at least one empty slot exists.

tasks.title: Cross Country
tasks.scenario: Three runners each overtake one runner on a specific terrain type. The course is a fixed sequence of terrain segments and the starting order is given. Predict the finishing order.
tasks.what_it_tests: Event-driven simulation where each event is an adjacent swap.
solution: Write the starting order.
For each segment in course order, apply the specialist's overtake (they move up one place).
Read the order after the last segment.
tasks.answer: Brown, Green, Pink. Trace: start Pink, Brown, Green; uphill Brown passes Pink; rocks Green passes Pink; downhill Pink passes Green; rocks Green passes Pink.
common_errors: Applying each runner's skill once regardless of how many segments of that terrain occur.
Reading the course in picture order rather than race order.
difficulty_drivers: Overtakes that are impossible when already first
hint_ladder: Write the order after each segment.
Which segment comes first in the race?
Does any terrain type appear twice?

generator_template.validity: Every specified overtake is possible when it occurs; final order differs from naive guess.

tasks.title: Animation
tasks.scenario: Five face pictures must be ordered before a known final frame so that each consecutive pair differs in exactly one feature (ears, whiskers, nose, teeth).
tasks.what_it_tests: Ordering states so neighbors differ by one attribute, by working back from a known end.
solution: List each picture's features.
Find the picture that differs from the final frame in one feature; it goes fifth.
Repeat backward, or forward from the picture that differs from the end in the most features.
tasks.answer: Big ears with wavy whiskers and small nose; small ears with wavy whiskers; straight whiskers with small nose; big pointed nose; rounder big nose (three teeth); then the final frame with two teeth.
common_errors: Missing small differences such as nose shape or tooth count.
Allowing two features to change in one step.
hint_ladder: Which picture is closest to the last frame?
Count the teeth.
Which picture is furthest from the last frame?

generator_template.validity: A unique Hamming-1 path exists from the start through all frames to the given end.

tasks.title: Fair Share
tasks.scenario: Water-jug puzzle: containers of 4 (full), 3 and 1 (empty). A pour stops when the source empties or the target fills. Split the liquid evenly between the 4-owner and the owner of the other two, in the fewest pours.
tasks.what_it_tests: State-space search with constrained operators and proof of minimality.
solution: Goal: 2 in the 4-container and 2 spread across the others.
List states after one and two pours; none reaches the goal.
Find a three-pour sequence.
tasks.answer: 3 pours, for example 4 to 3, then 3 to 1, then 1 to 4 (amounts go 4/0/0, 1/3/0, 1/2/1, 2/2/0). Also valid: 4 to 1, 1 to 3, 4 to 1.
common_errors: Thinking a pour can transfer any chosen amount.
Finding a working sequence without checking whether a shorter one exists.
hint_ladder: What amounts are possible after one pour?
After two?
Which state is one pour away from 2 and 2?

generator_template.validity: Goal reachable; minimum length is 3-5; at least two shortest solutions or exactly one, as chosen.

tasks.title: Walnut Animals
tasks.scenario: Figures are made of nuts joined by sticks. Someone bends them without removing sticks. Which bent figure can be bent back into the reference figure?
tasks.what_it_tests: Graph isomorphism using invariants rather than appearance.
solution: Count nodes in the reference (7).
Find each node's number of sticks: one node with 4, one with 3, the rest 1, and the two hubs joined.
Reject options with the wrong count or degrees; confirm hub adjacency.
tasks.answer: The figure with two joined hubs, one touching 4 sticks and one touching 3 (the fourth option in the Benjamin set).
common_errors: Matching by overall shape.
Counting nodes but not degrees.
difficulty_drivers: Distractors with the right count but wrong degrees
Distractors with right degrees but wrong adjacency
hint_ladder: Does bending change how many sticks touch a nut?
Count the nuts in each option.
Find the busiest nut in each.

generator_template.validity: One option isomorphic; distractors fail on node count, degree sequence, or hub adjacency.

tasks.title: Binary Hotel
tasks.scenario: A large den of numbered rooms is explored one room at a time with left, right and back exits. Find a target room number.
tasks.what_it_tests: Discovering that the den is a binary search tree and searching it efficiently.
solution: Notice that left rooms are smaller and right rooms larger.
At each room, go left if the target is smaller, right if larger.
Stop at the target.
tasks.answer: From the start room 5499: left 3251, left 2126, left 1560, left 1281, right 1420, left 1352, left 1318, right 1337. Eight moves.
common_errors: Wandering without a rule.
Going right when the current number is larger than the target.
hint_ladder: Go left once and right once from the start. What do you notice about the numbers?
Is the target bigger or smaller than this room?

generator_template.validity: Target present; rule never stated.

tasks.title: Dream Dress
tasks.scenario: Four shops each sell three dresses. A buyer needs short sleeves, more than three buttons, and stars on the sleeves. Which shop has it?
tasks.what_it_tests: AND-filtering with strict inequality and attribute location.
solution: Check every dress against all three conditions.
Reject dresses with exactly three buttons, long sleeves, or stars only on the body.
tasks.answer: B&B (its dark navy dress).
common_errors: Accepting exactly three buttons.
Accepting stars elsewhere on the dress.
Stopping at the first dress that meets two conditions.
difficulty_drivers: Near-misses that fail exactly one condition
hint_ladder: Make a table with a column for each condition.
Does three count as more than three?
Where exactly are the stars?

generator_template.validity: Exactly one item meets all conditions.

tasks.title: Quick Beaver Code
tasks.scenario: Square grids encode numbers: cells are valued 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on, starting at the bottom-right and moving left then up. A worked 3x3 example is given. Which of four 4x4 grids encodes the largest number?
tasks.what_it_tests: Binary place value and comparing numbers by most significant bit.
solution: The top-left cell is worth the most (2^15 in a 4x4 grid).
It outweighs all other cells combined.
Pick the only grid with that cell filled.
tasks.answer: The grid with its top-left cell filled.
common_errors: Counting filled cells.
Adding all values the long way and making arithmetic errors.
Reading the ordering from the top-left.
difficulty_drivers: Whether options tie on the top bits
hint_ladder: Which cell is worth the most?
Can all the other cells together be worth more than it?

generator_template.validity: Unique maximum.

tasks.title: Drawing Patterns
tasks.scenario: A pen moves on a grid and fills each cell it visits. A loop body of up to seven moves runs six times. Fill the body to draw a two-row zigzag.
tasks.what_it_tests: Decomposing a pattern into a repeating unit and writing a loop body.
solution: Find the period of the target: four columns.
Trace one period from the start cell.
Write those moves as the body.
tasks.answer: Right, up, right, right, down, right (six instructions).
common_errors: Starting the unit at the wrong phase.
Forgetting that the start cell is already filled.
hint_ladder: Where does the pattern start to repeat?
How many columns does one repeat cover?
Trace one repeat from the starting square.

generator_template.validity: Body length at most slot count.

tasks.title: Beaver Logs
tasks.scenario: A river with islands; each possible dam segment between a bank and an island or between islands has a log cost. Build a bank-to-bank dam with the fewest logs.
tasks.what_it_tests: Shortest weighted path from one bank to the other.
solution: Treat banks and islands as nodes and segments as weighted edges.
Compute the cheapest cost to reach each island from one bank.
Take the cheapest total to the other bank.
tasks.answer: 15 logs: top bank to the upper-right island (4), to the large middle island (3), to the small triangular island (4), to the bottom bank (4).
common_errors: Starting with the cheapest single segment.
Missing a link between islands.
hint_ladder: What is the cheapest way to reach each island from the top bank?
Is the cheapest first step on the cheapest whole path?

generator_template.validity: Unique optimum; a greedy path is 1-2 worse.

tasks.title: Beaver Lunch
tasks.scenario: A tree diagram says how many of each container a tray can hold and how many of each food each container can hold. Which pictured lunch breaks the rules?
tasks.what_it_tests: Validating structures against a schema with minimum and maximum counts.
solution: Note the one required element: at least one napkin.
Check each lunch's counts at both levels.
tasks.answer: The lunch with a bowl of carrots and a plate with an egg but no napkin.
common_errors: Checking only upper limits.
Assuming an empty container is invalid.
hint_ladder: Is any item in the diagram required?
Which lunch lacks it?

generator_template.validity: Exactly one lunch invalid.

tasks.title: Chakhokhbili
tasks.scenario: A recipe has five timed steps, some depending on others. On one burner it takes 90 minutes. With more burners, which claim about time saved is false?
tasks.what_it_tests: Critical path and the limit of parallelism.
solution: Draw the dependencies.
Find the longest chain: 50 minutes.
Check each claim: two burners give 60, three give 50, four still 50.
tasks.answer: The claim that four burners save 50 minutes is false.
common_errors: Assuming more burners always help.
Ignoring dependencies.
hint_ladder: Which steps can happen at the same time?
What is the longest chain?

generator_template.validity: Exactly one claim false.

tasks.title: You Won't Find It
tasks.scenario: Words are encoded by reversing, rotating letters two places left, then shifting each letter forward one. Decode a five-letter message.
tasks.what_it_tests: Inverting a pipeline of transformations in reverse order.
solution: Shift each letter back one.
Rotate two places right.
Reverse.
tasks.answer: FLOOD.
common_errors: Undoing steps in forward order.
Rotating the wrong direction.
difficulty_drivers: Steps that are their own inverse
hint_ladder: What was done last?
Try encoding each option forward.

params.steps: 2-4 of reverse, rotate, shift, swap pairs

generator_template.validity: One option decodes correctly.

tasks.title: Throw the Dice
tasks.scenario: A nested IF/ELSE on three die rolls picks one of three play spots. Which triple leads to the innermost ELSE?
tasks.what_it_tests: Tracing nested conditionals including equality cases.
solution: The inner ELSE needs the first roll not greater than the second and the third not less than the first.
Check each triple.
tasks.answer: Three, three, three.
common_errors: Treating 'not greater' as 'less'.
Forgetting the outer condition must fail.
hint_ladder: To reach the last line, which test must fail?
What if two rolls are equal?

generator_template.validity: Exactly one triple reaches the target branch.

tasks.title: Theatre
tasks.scenario: Red, green and blue lights switch on and off in cycles of different lengths. A table maps each on/off combination to a colour. Give the stage colour for the first four minutes.
tasks.what_it_tests: Combining periodic signals and reading a truth table.
solution: Write each light's state per minute.
Look up each combination.
tasks.answer: Blue, cyan, magenta, white.
common_errors: Starting a light in the wrong phase.
Misreading the table row.
hint_ladder: Make a row for each light.
Is red on or off in minute one?

generator_template.validity: Sequence is not constant.

tasks.title: Stack Computer
tasks.scenario: A machine evaluates postfix expressions using a stack. Worked examples are shown. Enter the postfix form of 4*(8+3)-2.
tasks.what_it_tests: Converting infix to postfix and simulating a stack.
solution: Innermost first: 8 3 +.
Multiply by 4: 4 8 3 + *.
Subtract 2: 4 8 3 + * 2 -.
tasks.answer: 4 8 3 + * 2 - (evaluates to 42).
common_errors: Writing operators in infix order.
Placing 4 after the sum.
hint_ladder: Which operation happens first?
Where does 4 need to be when * arrives?

generator_template.validity: Integer result.

tasks.title: Super Power Family
tasks.scenario: A three-generation family diagram with arrows from each person to their parents. Each person has one trait of their own, and daughters take all of their mother's traits while sons take all of their father's. Pick the one true statement about who has which traits.
tasks.what_it_tests: Applying a recursive inheritance rule along typed edges (mother vs father) across two generations.
solution: Work out the grandparents' generation first: each has only their own trait.
For each parent, add the trait set of the same-sex parent above them.
For each child, add the same-sex parent's full set to their own trait.
Check each statement against the computed sets.
tasks.answer: The statement that the son whose own trait is riding has riding, painting and photography (photography from his father, painting from his father's father).
common_errors: Letting a son inherit through his mother's line.
Giving a child traits from both parents.
Stopping at one generation and missing what the parent inherited.
difficulty_drivers: Statements that are true for one sibling and false for another
hint_ladder: Start at the top of the diagram. What can each grandparent do?
Is this person a son or a daughter? Which parent do they copy?
Does the parent have anything they inherited too?

params.rule: same-sex inheritance or another typed rule

generator_template.validity: Exactly one statement true; each false statement reflects one rule error.

tasks.title: E-mail Scam
tasks.scenario: Someone answers a cheap rental listing online. The seller, who is out of town, offers to post the key after a large deposit is paid and attaches a copy of an ID to look trustworthy. Choose the best advice.
tasks.what_it_tests: Recognizing advance-payment fraud and why an ID copy is not verification.
solution: Note what cannot be checked: the flat, the seller, the ID.
Note the money is requested before anything is verified.
The safe advice is not to pay.
tasks.answer: Do not pay the deposit; it is very likely a scam.
common_errors: Trusting the ID copy as recourse.
Treating the deposit as refundable without any way to enforce it.
hint_ladder: Who could have sent this e-mail?
What does a copy of an ID prove?

generator_template.validity: One option is the safe action; each distractor trusts one red flag.

tasks.title: Irrigation System
tasks.scenario: Water runs downhill from a lake through branching and merging canals to six fields. Some forks have no gate and send water both ways; four gates each send water only left or only right. Set the gates so exactly a given set of fields gets water.
tasks.what_it_tests: Reachability through two-way switches in a network where channels merge, solved by propagating constraints from the fields that must stay dry.
solution: Find the fields that must stay dry and every route into them.
Each gate on such a route must point away from it; that fixes some gates.
Follow the consequences: a fixed gate decides which branch the next gate sees.
Set the remaining gate to reach the last required field.
tasks.answer: Upper-left gate left, lower-left gate right, upper-right gate right, lower-right gate left.
common_errors: Treating an ungated fork as a choice (it always feeds both sides).
Missing that two different gates can feed the same central channel.
Solving for the wanted fields first and flooding a dry one.
difficulty_drivers: Ungated forks that force water to unwanted fields
hint_ladder: Which fields must stay dry? Trace every way water could reach one of them.
Can water reach the middle field from more than one gate?
Once two gates are fixed, which fields already get water?

generator_template.validity: Exactly one gate setting irrigates the target set; brute force over 2^gates confirms.

tasks.title: Drawing Stars

solution: Count the dots.
From one dot, follow a line and count how many positions around the circle it lands from the start.
common_errors: Miscounting dots on a busy drawing.
Counting the dots skipped instead of the step (off by one).
difficulty_drivers: Stars that form several separate loops
hint_ladder: Number the dots around the circle.
From dot 1, which numbered dot does one line reach?

generator_template.validity: Rendered star matches n:k; distractors n±1 or k±1; include gcd>1 cases.

tasks.title: Popularity

tasks.what_it_tests: Deriving the right reach (2 steps) from the visibility rule and computing neighborhoods.
solution: A photo on a friend's page is seen by that friend and that friend's friends.

Count the two-step neighborhood for each candidate.
tasks.answer: Chio, whose two-step neighborhood covers all seven people.

Counting only direct friends.
hint_ladder: Where does this person's photo end up?

generator_template.validity: Unique maximum 2-hop reach that is not the unique maximum degree.

tasks.title: Word Chains
tasks.scenario: Six short words are joined whenever they differ by one letter. The labels are wiped and the cards are rearranged in a new layout with the same connections. Choose the labeling that puts every word back in the right place.
tasks.what_it_tests: Producing a graph isomorphism (the mapping), using a triangle and the shapes hanging off each hub.
solution: Find the degree-3 nodes in both drawings.
Find the triangle; it fixes the two hubs and one more word.
Tell the hubs apart by what hangs off them: a single leaf or a chain of two.
Place the rest and check every edge.
tasks.answer: The option with the leaf word at the top, attached to the hub that has a single leaf, and the two-word tail on the other hub.
common_errors: Matching by position in the drawing.
Swapping the two hubs.
Checking only some edges.
difficulty_drivers: Distractors that preserve degrees but not adjacency
hint_ladder: Which words have three connections?
Find three words all joined to each other.
One hub has one word hanging off it; the other has two in a row.

generator_template.validity: Graph has a unique labeled embedding up to automorphism; distractors break exactly one edge each.

tasks.title: Pirate Hunters
tasks.scenario: Two chasers and a runner on a ring of seven spaces, played on an interactive board. Chasers move one step to a free space; the runner jumps two spaces; the runner is caught only when both of its jump targets are occupied. Chasers move first. With best play, how fast can the runner be caught?
tasks.what_it_tests: Reasoning about optimal play for both sides, and recognizing that the answer can be 'never'.
solution: Notice the start already traps the runner, but chasers must move first and break the trap.
Check every chaser move: the runner always has a free jump.
Argue it repeats: whatever the chasers do, the runner restores an escape.
tasks.answer: The police can never force a capture.
common_errors: Playing a few games against a careless runner and reporting a short win.
Assuming chasers may pass.
difficulty_drivers: Whether the answer is a number or 'never'
Interactive board that invites trial play
hint_ladder: Before anyone moves, is the runner already trapped?

generator_template.validity: Answer from exhaustive game search; include positions where the answer is 'never'.

Symbols that appear on only one tile must face out; that rules out the third tile.

Matching opposite sides.

tasks.what_it_tests: Minimax in a misère placement game.
solution: Rule out holes next to your own pieces.
Of the rest, look ahead: the isolated leaf hole 7 is the only winning move.

Not considering the reply.

tasks.what_it_tests: Backward reasoning through an elimination tournament.
solution: Round 3: only G scored below Ada, so G was her partner.
Round 2: only D and F together are below Ada + G, so they were the other pair.
Check round 1: 72 beats 71.
tasks.answer: D, F and G (site explanation; brute force agrees).

Assuming teammates are high scorers.

tasks.title: Virus

tasks.what_it_tests: Simultaneous multi-source BFS with ties destroyed.
solution: The two start computers are neighbours, so both are destroyed on day 1.
Spread both fronts one day at a time; equal-day arrivals are destroyed.
tasks.answer: 6 (verified).

Spreading one virus fully first.
