observations: Cadet reuses seven Benjamin tasks: six move down one tier (Benjamin B to Cadet A, Benjamin C to Cadet B), and Bracelet stays at A.
Benjamin C tasks lean on representations (binary, trees, graphs); Cadet C tasks add procedural abstraction (conditionals, ciphers, scheduling, stacks).
Interactive formats appear at every tier; difficulty comes from concepts, not interface.

observations.reuse: The 2022-23 practice sets reuse heavily and in the same pattern as 2015: each group's tier C becomes the next group's tier B, and its tier B becomes the next group's tier A. Cadet tier B is exactly Benjamin tier C; Senior tier A is exactly Cadet tier C. Seven tasks appear in three groups. Of 60 slots across the four groups, 31 tasks are distinct.
what_changes_with_age: Benjamin: tracing state (swaps, runners), applying a local rule everywhere (tower, rug), checking constraints, and the first error-detection idea (parity map).
Cadet adds relative reasoning (walker's left/right, pointer rotation), indirection (nested list lookups), worst-case ordering, validity by invariants, and minimum-edit questions.
Junior hard tier needs a bound or a count before searching: area bound for packing, eliminations per question, a two-floor shortest path, a two-symbol grammar.
Senior hard tier: game minimax with a unique winning move, simultaneous two-source spread, edge-matching with rotation, backward reasoning through a tournament, recognising programs by output.

Compared with 2015: more grammar and parsing (Sailor Necklace, Mysteria), the first error-detection task (Pantry Map), logic gates (Lights On), bracket matching (Nuts and Bolts), and pointer/indexing (Lists). No 'computers and society' tasks in 2022-23.
implications_for_the_tutor: New gaps now covered: parity/error detection, grammars, logic gates, stack matching, indirection; add them to the concept graph before building families.
Several Benjamin and Cadet items have many valid answers (Lights On, Hangar Carousel, Favorite Movie). A generator must grade by evaluating the rule, not by comparing with one key.
Lists shows why distractors must be audited: there the left-to-right misreading lands on the right answer, so the item cannot detect that misconception.
Backward reasoning recurs at every level (Sailor Necklace, Lights On, Mysteria, Beaver Games); a tutor move 'start from the end' is worth a dedicated hint step.

progression.reuse: The 2015 example sets form one ladder. Tasks introduced as hard for a younger group reappear one tier easier for the next group up: Benjamin C to Cadet B, Cadet C to Junior B, Junior C to Senior B. Some recur across three groups (Stack Computer: Cadet C, Junior B, Senior A). Only about half of each upper set is new.
what_changes_with_age: Benjamin and Cadet hard tiers ask the student to execute or check something: trace a rule, follow a path, validate against a schema.
Junior hard tiers ask the student to reason about all possibilities: count every reading of a signal, compare everyone's reach, predict a game under best play.

Senior hard tiers ask for a count or an optimum with a proof-like justification: fewest rounds and why fewer is impossible, number of shortest routes, the unique complete tour, parsing a recursive notation.
Counting questions ('how many ways') do not appear below Junior. Questions whose answer is 'impossible' first appear at Junior.
A 'computers and society' strand (fraud, licensing) appears only from Junior up, always in the easiest tier.
implications_for_the_tutor: Use the Junior and Senior C tasks to set the ceiling for strong 12-year-olds; several of them (Popularity, Hard Fireworks, Bowl Factory, Kangaroo) need no new knowledge, only more careful reasoning.

Build new generator families around question types rather than size: count the ways (fireworks, chip), prove a minimum (spies), decide under optimal play (pirate hunters), find the unique tour (kangaroo).

Counting by partial sums (COUNTING_DP) is the single highest-value new concept: it unlocks Hard Fireworks, Building a Chip, and counting variants of the existing Lake Crossing and Rule Tracer families.

generator_principles: Every task has a unique answer that can be verified mechanically.
Distractors should fail exactly one condition, matching a known misconception.
Scale difficulty by size, subtlety and hidden rules, not by vocabulary.
Keep scenarios short; the concept should be discoverable from the picture.

misconceptions.description: Handles ties the wrong way: treats 'greater than' as 'greater than or equal to' (and the reverse). Typically from reading 'not greater than' as 'less than'.
misconceptions.remediation: Show a roll with two equal dice and ask whether each test is true or false.
misconceptions.look_again: Two of the dice are equal. Is 'greater than' true when the numbers are the same?

misconceptions.description: Reads the comparison backwards: checks whether the second-named die is greater instead of the first.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student say each test aloud with the actual numbers substituted in, left to right.
misconceptions.look_again: Read each test out loud with the real numbers in it. Which die has to be bigger?

misconceptions.description: Checks only the innermost IF and forgets that the outer test must have failed to get there.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: to reach this line, which earlier test had to be false? Trace from the top with a finger.
misconceptions.look_again: To reach that line, an earlier test had to be false. Did you check it?

misconceptions.description: Mixes up which die is the second and which is the third.
misconceptions.remediation: Label each die with its position number before evaluating any test.
misconceptions.look_again: Number the dice 1, 2, 3 from the left before you check any test. Did you use the right die each time?

misconceptions.description: Starts at the north shore and always takes the cheapest walkway available next, never reconsidering.
misconceptions.remediation: Show the greedy route's total next to the best route's total; ask where the cheap first step cost them later.
misconceptions.look_again: The cheapest first walkway is not always part of the cheapest crossing. Where did it lead you?

misconceptions.description: Same greedy habit, working back from the south shore.
misconceptions.remediation: Same as greedy from the start; point out that starting from the other side does not fix the habit.
misconceptions.look_again: Picking the cheapest walkway each time doesn't work from the south shore either. Add up the whole route.

misconceptions.description: Assumes the route with the fewest walkways is cheapest; counts hops instead of adding plank numbers.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to add the numbers on a short-looking route and on a longer one.
misconceptions.look_again: A route with fewer walkways can still need more planks. Did you add up the numbers?

misconceptions.description: Only considers routes that always head toward the far shore; never tries going back north to reach a cheaper walkway.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: is any rule saying you can never step back toward the start?
misconceptions.look_again: Does any rule say you must always head south? Try a route that steps back north.

misconceptions.description: Finds the right route but leaves out the walkway onto the far shore when adding.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student point to each walkway while adding, including the ones touching the shores.
misconceptions.look_again: Point to every walkway on your route as you add. Did you count the ones touching the shores?

misconceptions.description: Adds the cheapest walkway from each shore without checking that they connect through islands.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to trace the route they priced with a finger from shore to shore.
misconceptions.look_again: Trace your route with a finger from shore to shore. Does it really connect?

misconceptions.description: Answers a reach question with the node that has the most direct connections.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to list everyone who would actually see the item, step by step.

misconceptions.description: Finds one way to read a signal and assumes it is the only one.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask for a second reading starting with a different first word.
misconceptions.look_again: Could the signal start with a different first word?

misconceptions.description: Gives how long the shortest route is when asked how many shortest routes there are.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student restate the question, then ask what number goes at each grid point.
misconceptions.look_again: Read the question again. Does it ask how long the best route is, or how many best routes there are?

misconceptions.description: Wins a few games against a weak opponent and reports that as what happens under best play.
misconceptions.remediation: Play the opponent yourself and always choose the best escape.

misconceptions.description: Assumes a smaller group always finishes in no more rounds, missing the odd-group effect.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student try to schedule the smaller group in the example's number of rounds and see where it fails.

misconceptions.description: Counts individual swaps when asked for the number of passes (workers).
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what one worker does to the whole set as it goes by.

misconceptions.description: Uses one intermediate item for two recipes, forgetting it is consumed.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to physically lay out tokens and remove them as they are used.

misconceptions.description: Treats making a changed copy and distributing it as the same act under a license.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: who ends up with the changed version?

misconceptions.description: Never tries the shortest code word, so misses every reading that uses it.
misconceptions.remediation: At each point in the signal, have the student check every code word, shortest first.
misconceptions.look_again: At each spot in the signal, did you try every code word, even the shortest one?

misconceptions.description: Counts every reading attempt, including ones that get stuck before the end.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: does this reading use up the whole signal? Only complete readings count.
misconceptions.look_again: Does each reading you counted use up the whole signal, right to the last flash?

misconceptions.description: Treats two messages with the same words in a different order as the same message.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask whether 'east, fog' and 'fog, east' mean the same thing to the sailor.
misconceptions.look_again: Are 'east, fog' and 'fog, east' the same message? Count each order on its own.

misconceptions.description: Decodes the right words but puts them in the wrong order.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student mark where each word starts in the signal, left to right.
misconceptions.look_again: Mark where each word starts in the signal, left to right. Are your words in that order?

misconceptions.description: Misreads one flash (short for long or the reverse) while decoding.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student write the signal as S and L letters before decoding.
misconceptions.look_again: Write the signal as S and L letters first. Did you read every flash right?

misconceptions.description: Loses their place and skips a word.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student encode their answer back into flashes and compare lengths.
misconceptions.look_again: Turn your answer back into flashes. Is it as long as the signal?

misconceptions.description: Counts the intersections between the start and the goal instead of the routes.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student trace two different routes that pass through the same intersections in a different order.
misconceptions.look_again: Two routes can pass the same corners in a different order. Are you counting routes or corners?

misconceptions.description: Counts routes as if no intersections were closed.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student cross out every closed intersection and write 0 there before counting.
misconceptions.look_again: Cross out every closed corner first. Can a route go through one?

misconceptions.description: Finds the routes with one or two turns and misses the ones that zigzag.
misconceptions.remediation: Show one zigzag route of the same length and ask whether it is also shortest.
misconceptions.look_again: Could a zigzag route be just as short?

misconceptions.description: Counts the intersections on the route instead of the blocks between them (off by one).
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to count the street pieces the robot drives along, not the corners.
misconceptions.look_again: Count the blocks the robot drives along, not the corners it passes.

misconceptions.description: Gives the distance as if the robot could drive straight through closed intersections.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to trace the route with a finger and stop at the first closed intersection.
misconceptions.look_again: Trace your route with a finger. Does it go through a closed corner?

misconceptions.description: Always drives toward the goal and detours only when blocked, which can make a longer route.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to write the distance from the start at every intersection, nearest first.
misconceptions.look_again: Write how far each corner is from the start, nearest first. Is heading straight for the goal really shortest?

misconceptions.description: Finds one cheapest crossing and assumes it is the only one.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to look for a different route with the same total.
misconceptions.look_again: Is there a different route with exactly the same total?

misconceptions.description: Counts every possible crossing instead of only the cheapest ones.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student write each route's total next to it and cross out the expensive ones.
misconceptions.look_again: The question counts only crossings with the fewest planks. Did some of yours cost more?

misconceptions.description: Counts routes that are close to the cheapest as if they tied.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to add up the plank numbers exactly for each candidate route.
misconceptions.look_again: Add each route up exactly. Does every one you counted match the cheapest total?

misconceptions.description: Counts only the dice that the tests mention and forgets that an untested die can show any of 6 faces.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: does the rule ever look at this die? Then how many faces can it show for each roll you counted?
misconceptions.look_again: Is there a die the rules never look at? How many faces could it show?

misconceptions.description: Applies each swap or step to the starting picture instead of the current one.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student redraw the state after every step.

misconceptions.description: Picks a cell in an odd row without checking that its column is odd too.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask which rows AND which columns are odd, and look only where they cross.
misconceptions.look_again: Which rows are odd, and which columns are odd? Look where they cross.

misconceptions.description: Tries random forward derivations instead of undoing rules from the string.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask which rule could have produced the right-hand end, and undo it.
misconceptions.look_again: Work backward: which rule could have made the end of this necklace? Undo it and keep going.

misconceptions.description: Reads an 'only one' gate as 'at least one' and turns on both inputs.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what the gate does when both inputs are on.
misconceptions.look_again: What does an 'only one' box do when both of its wires are on?

misconceptions.description: Accepts a sequence because the numbers of openers and closers are equal, missing a point where the count goes negative.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student write the running count under each item.
misconceptions.look_again: Write the number of nuts in the bucket under each part. Does a bolt ever find it empty?

misconceptions.description: Evaluates a nested lookup from the outside in (left to right).
misconceptions.remediation: Ask which part of the expression can be worked out with what you already know.
misconceptions.look_again: Which part can you work out right now? Start with the innermost brackets.

misconceptions.description: Assumes the first item in an order must be the one at the start position.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask whether the rules say which plane has to leave first.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies questions by group size, not seeing that the winner must be carried into the next comparison.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask how many items one question rules out.

misconceptions.description: Searches for a packing without first computing what the best could be, so cannot tell when to stop.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask for the total area and which box sizes it allows.

misconceptions.description: Only considers raising ratings, missing that lowering a single top rating satisfies a person for every option.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask whether there is a way to make this friend content with any movie.

misconceptions.description: Uses map directions after the walker has turned, or absolute positions in a relative code.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to turn the map so the walker faces up.

misconceptions.description: Treats the two starting places as safe even when both colours reach them.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what flows into each starting tank in the first minute.
misconceptions.look_again: The starting tanks follow the same rules as every other tank. What flows into each of them, and when?

misconceptions.description: Spreads one colour all the way first and then the other, instead of both together, minute by minute.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student colour both fronts for minute 1, then for minute 2.
misconceptions.look_again: Both colours move in the same minute. Colour both of them for minute 1, then minute 2.

misconceptions.description: Counts the cost of switching floors once for a route that switches there and back.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask which floor B is on and how the route gets back there.

misconceptions.description: Works forward from the first round, where many outcomes are possible, instead of backward from the final.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask who Ada could have beaten in the last round.

misconceptions.description: Checks only that no bolt finds the bucket empty, forgetting that nuts left over at the end are also a failure.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask how many nuts are in the bucket when the belt is empty.
misconceptions.look_again: When the belt is empty, how many nuts are still in the bucket?

misconceptions.description: Checks the first few parts and stops, missing a problem near the end of the belt.
misconceptions.remediation: Keep the running count all the way to the last part.
misconceptions.look_again: Did you keep your count going all the way to the end of the belt?

misconceptions.description: Answers 'most nuts in the bucket at once' with the total number of nuts on the belt.
misconceptions.remediation: Bolts take nuts out as you go. Track the bucket after each part.
misconceptions.look_again: Bolts take nuts out as the belt moves. Follow the bucket after each part.

misconceptions.description: Looks only at the longest row of nuts in a row, forgetting nuts already waiting in the bucket.
misconceptions.remediation: Start each run of nuts from the number already in the bucket.
misconceptions.look_again: When a run of nuts starts, are some nuts already in the bucket?

misconceptions.description: Gives the number of nuts in the bucket at the end of the belt instead of the most at any moment.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: when was the bucket fullest?

misconceptions.description: Checks small parts and big parts separately, missing that a bolt must fit the nut on top of the pile.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw the pile of nuts and only let a bolt take the top one.
misconceptions.look_again: Only the nut on top of the pile can be taken. Does each bolt fit the nut on top?

misconceptions.description: Adds only enough parts to make the totals equal, ignoring bolts that came too early.
misconceptions.remediation: Count the bolts that found an empty bucket and the nuts left at the end separately.
misconceptions.look_again: Equal totals are not enough. Do any bolts arrive before there is a nut for them?

misconceptions.description: Counts only the extra nuts needed for early bolts and forgets nuts left over at the end.
misconceptions.remediation: After fixing the early bolts, how many nuts are still in the bucket at the end?
misconceptions.look_again: After fixing the early bolts, are any nuts still left in the bucket at the end?

misconceptions.description: Counts only the nuts left at the end and forgets bolts that found the bucket empty.
misconceptions.remediation: Run the count from the start: does it ever go below zero?
misconceptions.look_again: Run the count from the start. Does a bolt ever arrive with no nut waiting?

misconceptions.description: Counts boxes from 0, so reads one box to the right.
misconceptions.remediation: Point to the small number above each box and read the box under that number.
misconceptions.look_again: Read the small number above each box. Which box is box 1?

misconceptions.description: Counts box positions from the right-hand end of the row.
misconceptions.remediation: The box numbers are printed above the row; use them, starting from the left.
misconceptions.look_again: The box numbers are printed above the row. Which end does box 1 sit at?

misconceptions.description: Answers with the box number instead of the number inside the box.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: is this the box's label, or what is written inside it?
misconceptions.look_again: Is your answer the box's number, or what is written inside the box?

misconceptions.description: Does the inner lookup and stops, missing the outer one.
misconceptions.remediation: Count the brackets: each pair is one lookup to do.
misconceptions.look_again: Count the pairs of brackets. Each pair is one lookup. Did you do them all?

misconceptions.description: Uses the innermost row for every step instead of switching rows.
misconceptions.remediation: Before each step, say which row's name is in front of the bracket.
misconceptions.look_again: Before each step, which row's name is in front of the bracket?

misconceptions.description: Asked which start gives the target, runs the expression forward from the target instead of working backward.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: which box of the outer row holds the target? Then where is that number in the inner row?
misconceptions.look_again: Work backward: which box in the outer row holds the target?

misconceptions.description: Works backward through the outer row only and stops.
misconceptions.remediation: You found the box in the outer row. That box number came from the inner row: find it there.
misconceptions.look_again: You found a box in the outer row. Where does that box number come from in the inner row?

misconceptions.description: Reads a 'both' box as if one wire were enough.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: does this box need one wire or both wires to send a signal on?
misconceptions.look_again: Does that box need one wire on, or both wires on?

misconceptions.description: Finds a set that works but uses more beavers than needed.
misconceptions.remediation: Work backward from the bulb and, at each box, choose the cheapest way to make it send a signal.
misconceptions.look_again: The bulb lights. Could it light with fewer buttons pressed?

misconceptions.description: Finds one working set and stops, as if there were only one answer to count.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: is there another set that also works? Try listing them in order.
misconceptions.look_again: Is there another set of buttons that also works? Try listing them in order.

misconceptions.description: Adds beads at either end, when the rule says which end.
misconceptions.remediation: Read the rule again: which end do the new beads go on? Check the end of the necklace first.
misconceptions.look_again: Read the rule again. Which end do the new beads go on?

misconceptions.description: Reads 'one bead at each end' as two beads on the same end.
misconceptions.remediation: Point to both ends of the necklace. The rule puts one new bead at each.
misconceptions.look_again: Does the rule add both beads to one end, or one bead at each end?

misconceptions.description: Lets a rule put its new objects in any order.
misconceptions.remediation: The rule's objects always come out in the order shown, left to right.
misconceptions.look_again: A rule's new objects always come out in the order shown. Did you keep that order?

misconceptions.description: Applies a rule to an object of the wrong kind.
misconceptions.remediation: Each rule changes only the kind of object on its left side. Which kind is this?
misconceptions.look_again: Each rule changes only the kind of object on its left side. Was it that kind?

misconceptions.description: Counts necklaces of every length up to N instead of exactly N beads.
misconceptions.remediation: Each necklace in the count must have exactly the number of beads asked for.
misconceptions.look_again: Does every necklace you counted have exactly the number of beads asked for?

misconceptions.description: Picks a crossing that already holds a dot, when the question is where a dot was rubbed out.
misconceptions.remediation: A rubbed-out dot left an empty shelf. Can it be a shelf that still shows a dot?
misconceptions.look_again: A rubbed-out dot leaves an empty shelf. Can it be a shelf that still shows a dot?

misconceptions.description: Makes every row even but forgets to check the columns.
misconceptions.remediation: Now count each column too, including the check row at the bottom.
misconceptions.look_again: Every row is even now. Count each column too, including the check row at the bottom.

misconceptions.description: Makes every column even but forgets to check the rows.
misconceptions.remediation: Now count each row too, including the check column on the right.
misconceptions.look_again: Every column is even now. Count each row too, including the check column on the right.

misconceptions.description: Fills the check row and column but gets the shared corner wrong.
misconceptions.remediation: The corner belongs to both the last row and the last column. Count both.
misconceptions.look_again: The corner shelf belongs to both the last row and the last column. Does it work for both?

misconceptions.description: Runs the spread for one minute too few or one too many.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student write 'minute 1', 'minute 2' and so on, and list what changes under each.
misconceptions.look_again: Write 'minute 1', 'minute 2' and so on, with what changes under each. How many minutes does the question ask about?

misconceptions.description: Lets the paint run through every connected tank at once, ignoring that it moves one pipe per minute.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask how far the paint can get in the very first minute.
misconceptions.look_again: Paint moves through one pipe each minute. How far can it get in the first minute?

misconceptions.description: Counts only the tanks the paint flowed into and leaves out the tank it was poured into.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what colour the starting tank is at the end.
misconceptions.look_again: What colour is the tank the paint was poured into?

misconceptions.description: Thinks a tank that already has a colour can never change, so only tanks reached by both colours in the same minute turn to mud.
misconceptions.remediation: Find two neighbouring tanks of different colours and ask what flows into each one in the next minute.
misconceptions.look_again: Find an orange tank and a blue tank joined by a pipe. What does each push into the other next minute?

misconceptions.description: Lets mud keep pushing colour into its neighbours, so mud spreads.
misconceptions.remediation: Reread the rule about mud with the student, then redo the minute where the first mud appears.
misconceptions.look_again: Read the rule about mud again. Can a mud tank push paint anywhere?

misconceptions.description: Counts the mud tanks as if they still had the asked colour.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to name each tank they counted and say its colour at the end.
misconceptions.look_again: Name each tank you counted and say its colour at the end. Is any of them mud?

misconceptions.description: Mixes up the two counts: reads 'right spot' as 'wrong spot' and the other way round.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student say each clue in full words ('one symbol is in exactly the right spot') before testing a code.
misconceptions.look_again: Say one clue in full words: how many symbols are in exactly the right spot, and how many are in a wrong spot?

misconceptions.description: Checks how many symbols a guess shares with the code, but not whether each one is in the right spot.
misconceptions.remediation: For each clue, have the student point to each shared symbol and say whether it sits in the same spot in both.
misconceptions.look_again: Pick a symbol your code shares with a guess. Is it on the same wheel in both, or a different one?

misconceptions.description: Stops checking a code before trying it against every clue, so a code that breaks one clue looks right.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student tick off each clue as they test a code, and only accept a code with every clue ticked.
misconceptions.look_again: Test your code against every clue, ticking each one off. Does it really agree with all of them?

misconceptions.description: Ignores a clue that says nothing is right, so a symbol that clue rules out stays in the code.
misconceptions.remediation: Start with the 'nothing is right' clue: have the student cross out every symbol in it before using any other clue.
misconceptions.look_again: One guess has nothing right. Did you cross out every symbol in it?

misconceptions.description: When the two bricks below are different colours, copies one of them instead of using the third colour.
misconceptions.remediation: Point to two different bricks and ask: if the top must differ from both, which colour is left?
misconceptions.look_again: Find a brick that rests on two different colours. Can it match either of them, or must it be the third colour?

misconceptions.description: Counts only the bricks the student worked out and leaves out the bottom row that was given.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the student to point at every brick of that colour, starting with the bottom row.
misconceptions.look_again: Point to every brick of that colour, starting with the bottom row. Did you count them all?

misconceptions.description: When the two bricks below match, puts a different colour on top, as if every brick had to change.
misconceptions.remediation: Reread the rule: 'all the same' is allowed. Ask what goes on top of two red bricks.
misconceptions.look_again: Find a brick that rests on two bricks of the same colour. Does the rule let all three be the same?

misconceptions.description: Adds up every friend's friends without noticing that some people hear the news twice, or are the sender.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student tick each person once, the first time they hear it.
misconceptions.look_again: Some people hear the news from two friends. Did you tick each person only once?

misconceptions.description: Counts the person who had the news as one of the people who hear it.
misconceptions.remediation: Reread the question: does the sender hear their own news from someone?
misconceptions.look_again: Read the question again. Does the person with the news count as hearing it?

misconceptions.description: Makes friends with a person the news misses, which reaches that one person but not the others it misses.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask: a new friend tells their own friends too. Whose friends cover everyone who is missed?
misconceptions.look_again: A new friend also tells all of their own friends. Whose friends cover everyone who is missed?

misconceptions.description: Assumes the person with the most friends spreads news the furthest.
misconceptions.remediation: Count two steps out from the most-friended person and from another person, and compare.
misconceptions.look_again: Count two steps out from the person with the most friends. Does that really reach the most people?

misconceptions.description: Counts only the sender's own friends and forgets that each friend passes the news on.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what each friend does with the news after hearing it.
misconceptions.look_again: The friends hear it first. What does each of them do with the news next?

misconceptions.description: Counts only the people reached in the second step and leaves out the friends who heard it first.
misconceptions.remediation: Have the student list step one and step two separately, then add both lists.
misconceptions.look_again: Did you count the friends who heard it first, as well as the people they told?

misconceptions.description: Lets the news travel a third step (or further), past the friends of friends.
misconceptions.remediation: Reread the rule: nobody passes the news on a third time. Mark where step two ends.
misconceptions.look_again: Mark the friends, then their friends. Does anyone tell the news a third time?

misconceptions.description: Assumes the frog must finish on the stone at the far end of the row.
misconceptions.remediation: Follow the hops one at a time and see where the frog really stops.
misconceptions.look_again: Does the frog have to finish at the far end? Follow its hops one at a time and see where it really stops.

misconceptions.description: Makes a hop that is not one of the two allowed sizes, often one spot too short or too long.
misconceptions.remediation: Count the spots on every hop, water spots included, before moving on.
misconceptions.look_again: Count the spots on each hop, water spots too. Is every hop exactly the right size?

misconceptions.description: Lets the frog land on a stone it has already visited.
misconceptions.remediation: Cross off each stone as the frog lands on it; a crossed-off stone cannot be used again.
misconceptions.look_again: Does the frog land on any stone more than once?

misconceptions.description: Follows one choice of hop until the frog is stuck and stops there, instead of going back to the last choice and trying the other hop.
misconceptions.remediation: When the frog gets stuck with stones left, go back to the last stone where it had two hops and try the other one.
misconceptions.look_again: The frog got stuck with stones left. Where was the last stone it had two hops to choose from? Try the other one.

misconceptions.description: Mixes up the two hops: goes forward by the back size and back by the forward size.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the rule as two arrows (forward a, back b) and check each hop against it.
misconceptions.look_again: Which hop goes forward, and which goes back? Check each hop against the rule again.
